newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil leads energy prices on year-end rally.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil leads energy prices on year-end rally.

text.p: Oil prices surged Tuesday as traders focused on cold weather in Europe and ignored the outlook for moderate temperatures in the Northeast.
The buying in heating oil helped push overall commodities indexes higher on the final trading day of 1996.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures prices closed 1.41 points higher for the day at 239.61, as copper, natural gas and other markets rose as well.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil for January delivery led energy prices higher, surging 2.27 cents a gallon to close at 72.84 cents on its final trading day.

The National Weather Service's latest six-to-10-day forecast Monday called for above-normal to much-above-normal temperatures for the eastern half of the nation, including Texas, between Jan. 5 and 9. That contributed to selling pressure.
But strong prices Tuesday in Europe for heating fuel countered the local selling pressure.
Private weather forecasters said temperatures would be below normal in the Northeast this week before rising next week, adding strength to the heating oil rally, dealers said.
Keying off heating oil, January gasoline ended up 1.06 cents a gallon at 70.67 cents, while February crude rose 55 cents a barrel to end at $25.92 after reaching a contract high of $25.97.
February natural gas futures ended 8 cents higher to close at $2.757 per million British thermal units, buoyed by the rally in the other fuels.
At the COMEX division of the New York Mercantile Exchange, March copper ended up 2 cents a pound at 100.25 cents as traders squared positions ahead of the year's end in reduced volume.

"We are becoming much less bearish about the short-term outlook for copper prices," said Merill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold. "Chinese demand combined with normal growth in the rest of the world is likely to consume almost all of the extra copper coming on stream, with the result that we are unlikely to see much of a supply surplus develop," he said.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, January lumber futures rose the daily limit of $10 per thousand board feet to $424.70 after the report of a jump in new home sales.
The Commerce Department reported a 14.2 percent jump in single-family home sales in November, the largest rise since April 1993. Cash markets also were strong.

Pork prices also were mostly higher after rising the daily allowable limits on Monday. April lean hogs rose 1.50 cents per pound to 76.225 cents and February pork bellies ended 1.925 cents higher at 82.350 cents a pound.

The government's pig crop report Friday continued to be the primary motivator for buying, particularly in deferred hog contracts and pork bellies. The report indicated a drop of 4 percent from a year ago in the hog herd as of Dec. 1.
But ample hogs for current slaughter needs and steady to lower cash hog prices Tuesday at Midwest markets prompted the selling of February hogs, which closed at 79.225 cents, down 0.275 cent.

Grain markets at the Chicago Board of Trade were quiet in an abbreviated session. Good weather in Argentina and Brazil continued to prompt selling, while some buying in corn by grain firm Cargill was tied to talk it may ship grain to North Korea if the Treasury Department grants permission.
January soybeans ended down 3-3/4 cents a bushel at $6.90-1/2, March wheat fell 3/4 cent a bushel to $3.81-1/4, and March corn closed unchanged at $2.58-1/4 a bushel.
